meters.label: Digits in the backtracking step count

frames.narration: First the simple case: searching a text of 1,000 a's for aaaaaaaaab. A naive search slides the pattern along and compares. At each of the 991 positions the first 9 characters match and the last fails, so it makes 9,910 comparisons. KMP never moves back in the text and makes 2,008.
Now a signup form checks a field with ^(a+)+$. On inputs that match, such as 10 a's, the engine finishes in 12 steps. Every test passes and the pattern ships.
A user sends 10 a's and a b. It does not match, and the engine needs 2,047 steps to prove it. At 15 a's it is 65,535 steps, at 20 a's 2,097,151. Each extra character doubles the work.

Why: n a's can be split between the inner and the outer repeat in 2^(n-1) ways. A match stops at the first way. A near miss fails after every way is tried, and the engine returns to each choice in turn. The step count is 2^(n+1) - 1, checked against the matcher up to n = 20.

At 1 ns per step: 30 a's is 2,147,483,647 steps, about 2 seconds. 40 a's is 2,199,023,255,551 steps, about 37 minutes. 50 a's is 2,251,799,813,685,247 steps, about 26 days of one core, from a request the user can send in one second.

Fix 1: remove the ambiguity. ^a+$ accepts the same strings in only one way and needs 21 steps at n = 20. The other pattern, (a|aa)+, is not a fix: it grows like Fibonacci numbers, 75,022 steps at n = 20.

Fix 2: a matcher that follows all positions at once instead of backtracking. For the nested pattern at n = 20 it takes 41 steps, and at n = 50 it takes 101: the cost grows with the length of the text, not with 2 to the n.

Where the backtracking engine stays, limit the input length, set a match timeout and test patterns with near-miss inputs, not only with matching ones. Linear search and linear regex engines have a worst case you can state; backtracking has one you must find.
